title: His brother David
hookLine: his brother drowned at sea on a trading voyage; Maimonides grieved for years

cards: Two brothers, one house. The older one, Moses, sits with his books. The younger one, David, packs for a long trip.
He is a merchant, and the family lives on what he earns; that's what lets his brother study and write without worrying about bread.
David sets out by sea, heading for India, carrying his own money and money that others have trusted him with. And then the ship goes down.
Today, the brother of the Rambam, and what the Rambam himself wrote about his grief.

teach.h: A LETTER TO AN OLD FRIEND.
teach.b: We know this mostly from the Rambam's own words. Years later he wrote to an old friend, a judge in the land of Israel who had once traveled with him.
The friend had complained that the Rambam hadn't written in a long time. The answer is deeply personal.
The worst thing that ever happened to him, he explains, was the death of his brother, who drowned in the Indian Ocean. For about a year afterward he lay ill, in grief, close to despair.

David had been raised on his knees; they had studied together; David had carried the family's business so that he could stay at his desk. David left a young widow and a little daughter, and the Rambam took them in.
Then comes the line that gives today its name.
Even now, after all this time, he writes, he is still mourning. When he sees David's handwriting or one of his books, the grief comes back.
Notice who is saying this: the writer of a vast code of law and a demanding book of philosophy, a man who wrote about the mind and its control of feeling. And he doesn't pretend.
He tells his friend plainly that the loss still lives in him. Jewish mourning has its own rhythm: the first week, the first month, the first year, and the yearly day of remembrance after that.
The rhythm doesn't say grief ends.
It gives grief a shape to walk through, and the Rambam's letter shows a scholar walking through it slowly, and saying so.

how: Jewish mourning moves in stages, with shiva in the first week, shloshim through the first month, a year of saying Kaddish for a parent, and a yahrzeit candle lit on each anniversary of the death.

games.q: you are the Rambam. an old friend writes, hurt that you have not written in a long time. what do you tell him?
o: blame your workload and change the subject.
tell him plainly about your brother's death and that you still grieve.
send a short legal ruling instead.
games.why: he wrote back plainly, describing David's death and saying he still mourned years later.

practice: Bring to mind someone close, a sibling or an old friend, living or gone, and picture one ordinary thing about them: their handwriting, a laugh, the way they packed a bag.
If grief comes, let it sit beside you; it doesn't need fixing, and if they're living, think of one thing you'd like them to know. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words.

wordCard.voice: David. The Rambam's younger brother, a merchant lost at sea, still mourned years later in his brother's own letter. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: David, the brother's name, the same name as the biblical king.

carryVoice: Your line: grief takes years. Even the Rambam still missed his brother, long after. Go gently, and see you tomorrow.
